title: Liking Yourself Too Much Can Hinder Personal Growth
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Opening with Ginni Rometty's line that growth and comfort never coexist, this article names a subtle form of complacency: leaders who, after real success, become quietly enamored with their own competence and stop seeking real challenge. The author argues this self-satisfaction is one of the most common and least recognized barriers to continued growth, precisely because a healthy dose of self-regard is necessary and easy to mistake for excess. The recommended antidote is deliberately seeking out unfamiliar tasks and candid feedback that puts strengths back into perspective. The piece ends with a memorable 'recipe' for staying uncomfortable: candid feedback, new challenges, and new experience.
points: Genuine growth requires discomfort, but success often breeds a quiet self-satisfaction that blocks further development.
Leaders can become 'uncoachable' specifically because they like themselves and their track record too much to keep learning.
The fix isn't rejecting self-regard entirely, but pairing it with deliberate exposure to unfamiliar, uncomfortable challenges.
Seeking candid feedback that puts one's strengths in perspective helps counteract the pull of comfort.
quotes: You can’t accept who you are right now and grow at the same time.
Or, as former IBM Ceo Ginni Rometty liked to say, “Growth and comfort never coexist.
Of the many pernicious ways comfort weasels its way into the mindset of leaders, perhaps none is more common than the idea of liking oneself a bit too much.
In fact, examine the most uncoachable leaders and you are likely to find people who have stopped learning because they like themselves too much.
Two parts candid feedback, three parts new challenges, and one part new experience. That’s a cocktail worth consuming.
